Q: CSS and SEO Question A:

Yes, this setup is generally fine for SEO as long as the text inside the <span> is still in the HTML and only visually hidden with CSS. Search engines like Google can still read it.

Just avoid:

  • Hiding text with display:none or visibility:hidden purely to manipulate rankings

  • Using images instead of meaningful text (no text = weaker SEO)

Best practice:
Keep the text accessible (for SEO + accessibility) and use CSS for styling only.

Q: Which services are typically required to scale a LAMP stack for high-traffic production environments? A:

I first make sure my database is normalized and has the obvious indexes for single columns which I know are essential. I am conservative here. Indexes can take up a lot of resources and bad indexing can even slow things down.

Then I use my own code to check how much execution time is taken up by which queries, after the code has run for some time in simulated normal usage. Any database profiling tool will do here. I concentrate my efforts on those queries that take up most of the time. Some queries just have to run, like for the session data, which I store in the database. Other time-consuming queries should probably be optimized.

The optimization can vary. Sometimes adding an index for a single, or multiple, columns is enough, sometimes the query can become part of another, and sometimes the data can be cached in some way. It all depends on the query itself. This step requires experience.

I then iterate several times through this optimization process, all the while keeping an eye on the total execution time of the web pages. Faster is better.

My pages have a "make time" and a "load time":

The first is the time needed before the first output to the client, and the latter is the overall load time as experienced by the user. SEO-sensitive pages need to be made in about 50 - 150 ms, and load within 1.0 second, on my own desktop from a web server which is about a 100 miles away. Google's PageSpeed Insights also gives good information. Pages that are not SEO-sensitive can be somewhat slower, but I prefer "make times" below 300 ms, and "load times" below 2 seconds. Users hate waiting.

If a page gets too slow, and all possible optimizations have been done, I sometimes split a page. A simple example is for instance a page where, among other things, the number of emails in a mailbox is reported. Connecting to the mail server, and retrieving this information is slow. So I use an AJAX call for this after the page was loaded. This is a common technique to speed up load times, which can also be used when database queries are slow.

While working on the optimization of the queries, I show on every page how many queries were used to build a page. The ORM I use does have build-in caching, and it also shows the number of cache hits and misses, if a query can be cached.

I try to minimize the number of queries, but you'll be surprised how many queries can be needed to create a decently complex page. 99 queries isn't even all that much, luckily half of them are cached. In the above image only 7 queries weren't cached that could have, and 1 update query was executed.

The details aren't all that important. What I am trying to convey is that optimizing code is a process you need to invest quite a bit of time in. There isn't a single magic solution. You go through each step several times, and then once more, all the time keeping an eye on the page loading times. Sometimes the code needs rewriting, don't be afraid of that. The more you do this, the better you get at it.

Q: How do I split a string in groups of 2 characters in powershell without delimiters? A:

For readers (like me) wondering what magical voodoo is going on in Theo's answer, the default behaviour of the Split operator is to use a regular expression to evaluate the delimiter (hence '..'). But, also by default, the delimiter is omitted from the results, so splitting at 2 characters doesn't work:

PS > '1234302392323' -split '..'
   <-- substring (empty)
   <-- substring (empty)
   <-- substring (empty)
   <-- substring (empty)
   <-- substring (empty)
   <-- substring (empty)
3  <-- substring

To preserve the delimiter, it must be enclosed in parentheses (hence '(..)'):

PS > '1234302392323' -split '(..)'
   <-- substring (empty)
12 <-- delimiter
   <-- substring (empty)
34 <-- delimiter
   <-- substring (empty)
30 <-- delimiter
   <-- substring (empty)
23 <-- delimiter
   <-- substring (empty)
92 <-- delimiter
   <-- substring (empty)
32 <-- delimiter
3  <-- substring

Finally, -ne '' filters out the empty substrings:

PS > '1234302392323' -split '(..)' -ne ''
12 <-- delimiter
34 <-- delimiter
30 <-- delimiter
23 <-- delimiter
92 <-- delimiter
32 <-- delimiter
3  <-- substring

Q: What is difference between Base64 and Multipart? A:

Multipart is a part of the HTTP protocol. See

What is an HTTP multipart request?

Base64 is a way to convert arbitrary content into a serializable form for transmission.

Q: What is an HTTP multipart request? A:

I have found an excellent and relatively short explanation here.

A multipart request is a request containing several packed requests inside its entity.

Q: Arm Assembly proper way to PUSH POP link register and pc in a subroutine and calling a subroutine within a subroutine A:

There are three cases that you should be aware of.

  1. Leaf: void foo(void) {};
  2. Tail call: int foo(void) { return bar(); };
  3. Intermediate: int foo(void) { int i; i = bar() + 4; return i; };

There are many ways to implement these calls. Below are some samples and are not the only way to implement epilogue and prologue in ARM assembler.

LEAF funtions

Many functions are the leaf type and do not require saving of the lr. You simply use the bx lr to return. For example,

SubRoutine:
  PUSH {r1,r2}
  //code that changes r1 and r2
  POP {r1,r2}
  bx lr

Also, it is typical that r1 and r2 are used to pass parameters and a SubRoutine is free to use/destroy them.ARM calling conventions This will be the case if you call 'C' function from assembler. So typically, no one would save r1 and r2 but as it is assembler you can do what ever you like (even if it is a bad idea). So actually the example is only bx lr if you follow the standard.

Tail Call

If your function is a leaf except for a final call to another function you can use the following short cut,

Sub_w_tail:
// Save callee-saved regs (for whatever calling convention you need)
// Leave LR as is.
// ... do stuff
B  tail_call

The LR is saved by the caller to Sub_w_tail and you just jump directly to tail_call which returns to the original caller.

Intermediate function

This is the most complex. Here is a possible sequence,

SubRoutine:
   PUSH {r1,r2,r3,lr}

  //code that *possibly* changes r1 and r2
  bl AnotherRoutine (where bx lr will be used to return from it)

  // more code
  POP {r1,r2,r3,pc}   // returns to caller of 'SubRoutine'

Some details of an older calling convention are in the ARM Link and frame registers question. You can use this convention. There are many different ways to perform the epilogue and prologue in ARM assembler. Refer to APCS and AAPCS documents for details.

The last is quite complex; or at least tedious to code. It is a lot better to let a compiler determine what registers to use and what to place on the stack. However, usually you only need to know how to code the first (LEAF function) when writing assembler. It is most productive only to code an optimized sub-routine called from a higher level language in assembler. It is useful to know how all of them work to understand compiled code. You should also consider inline assembler so you don't have to deal with these nuances.

Q: fatal error: opencv2/xfeatures2d.hpp: No such file or directory A:

You have to include cmake compilation flag to opencv OPENCV_EXTRA_MODULES_PATH and set it to the opencv_contrib/modules.

cmake -DOPENCV_EXTRA_MODULES_PATH=../opencv_contrib/modules
